name: Appeal to Probability Fallacy
description: People treat a possible or vaguely probable scenario as if it were effectively certain or already true. The move is common in speculation, risk talk, and product storytelling: 'it could happen' quietly becomes 'it will happen.'
design_relevance_note: Relevant to AI risk framing, speculative roadmap narratives, fraud/security warnings, and scenario planning: teams can smuggle inevitability into decisions by treating a merely possible outcome as if it were the default future.
myth_risk_note: No rigorous peer-reviewed empirical backing found in this pass or the existing corpus. This is a logical-fallacy label discussed in informal-logic/rhetoric contexts, not a tested psychological phenomenon with experimental validation -- consistent with this taxonomy's Law-of-Triviality/Jakob's-Law precedent for aphorism-only entries.
prevalence_note: Mostly a logic and critical-thinking classroom term; it shows up only occasionally in product or UX conversations, usually inside broader risk or reasoning critiques rather than as a standard design heuristic.
